claims.statement: The homelab bring-up runbook is a from-scratch, phase-ordered procedure for a single headless host whose phases assume the prior phase's state (e.g. the two service users and their networks/volumes must exist before Forgejo or the app stacks are deployed), so a partial rebuild cannot skip ahead; it provisions Ubuntu Server LTS with firmware virtualization/IOMMU enabled and full-disk LVM, then hardens SSH to key-only, sets ufw default-deny inbound, and reaches the host over Tailscale only.

The host runs two unprivileged service users (`ci` and `prod`), each with its own rootless dockerd at its own socket and its own data root under its home, and the rootful docker.service is disabled — this is the isolation boundary that keeps a CI breakout from reaching prod or the host as root. The prod daemon hosts the long-lived services (Forgejo, Komodo, the RustFS-backed Nx cache, monitoring), while the CI daemon runs build/test jobs.

Rootless Docker must be installed for each service user from a `machinectl shell <user>@` session (`systemd-container` provides it), not `sudo -iu`/`su`: the setup tool needs a real systemd user session to install the auto-start unit, and the wrong session type silently falls back to a manual-start mode (it prints "systemd not detected" and points XDG_RUNTIME_DIR at the user's home instead of /run/user/<uid>). Linger must be enabled so the user manager and daemons run without an active login.

Each service user must have exactly one non-overlapping subordinate UID/GID range; `useradd -m` already assigns one, so the normal action is verification only. Adding a second range via `usermod --add-subuids` creates an overlap that breaks rootless Docker's user-namespace mapping with an opaque `newuidmap: write to uid_map failed: Invalid argument` error.

Cgroup delegation must be enabled at the systemd `user@.service` level (`Delegate=cpu cpuset io memory pids` via a drop-in, then reboot); otherwise rootless Docker only enforces memory/pids limits and silently ignores CPU/IO limits, which breaks the CI-vs-prod performance isolation that host cgroup caps on the user slices provide.

Although the two rootless daemons are isolated at the daemon and filesystem level, they still publish into the same host's port space, which is the origin of the prod↔CI port-collision class: a prod bind on 0.0.0.0 collides with a CI bind on the same port regardless of the CI host_ip, which is why prod admin/UI ports live in a reserved range enforced by the required `check-prod-ci-port-collision.mjs` guardrail.

This forge build (15.0.3+gitea-1.22.0) exposes no Actions-artifact API — `GET /api/v1/repos/.../actions/artifacts` is a missing route (404), not an empty result — so an `upload-artifact` APK is retrievable only by a human through the run page and only until it expires. `cd-deploy`'s `prod-apk` job therefore publishes every release APK to the generic package registry as package `mcm-app-android`, version `<expo.version>-<sha7>`, alongside a `.apk.sha256` sidecar in `sha256sum -c` format, using the existing `write:package` CI push token (no new token, no widened scope); retrieval uses a `read:package` token against `/api/packages` (not `/api/v1`).

Release-APK retention is count-based, not time-based: the measured universal release APK is 114,365,972 bytes (109 MB) on run #6036 and every deploy produces one, so `publish-apk.mjs` prunes to the newest 5 versions by `created_at` (≈550 MB ceiling) rather than a 30-day window, because a quiet month would delete every installable APK while a busy week would keep more than the disk affords. A version whose name ends in `-keep` is never pruned and does not consume a retention slot, which is the supported way to make a build outlive the window. The pruning keeps a version whose `created_at` fails to parse (deleting on a parse failure is the destructive direction), sorts by `created_at` rather than name (`1.10.0` sorts before `1.9.0` as a string, so name order would prune the newest first), and paginates the version listing because the forge defaults to 30 items ordered by name, making an unpaginated call a silent retention no-op.

`prod-apk` is deliberately non-blocking: no job `needs:` it, the publish step is `continue-on-error`, and `publish-apk.mjs` always exits 0 while printing `::error::` on every failure path, so a registry hiccup is visible in the job log without turning a deploy red. A re-upload of an already-published version is a 409 treated as "already published" rather than a failure, because the bytes are the same build of the same source.

The forge's `ubuntu-latest` runner label maps to `docker://node:22-bookworm`, a plain Node image running as root — not a GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner — so GitHub-hosted-runner recipes do not transfer. In particular `sudo` is not installed and is unnecessary (the kvm runner executes as the unprivileged `ci` user, which also has no sudo), and a copied `sudo …` line dies on its first word; with a customary `|| true` the step goes green having done nothing, which is exactly what `cd-deploy`'s `prod-apk` disk step did on every run it ever made.

Dropping `sudo` from the disk step is worse than leaving the no-op: measured 2026-09-15 with `docker run --rm node:22-bookworm`, `/usr/share/dotnet`, `/opt/ghc`, `/usr/local/.ghcup`, `/usr/share/swift` and `/usr/local/share/powershell` do not exist, and the one sizeable removable directory, `/usr/local/lib/node_modules` (19 MB), holds `corepack` and `npm`, which `pnpm/action-setup` resolves pnpm through two steps later — so a working `rm -rf` would break the job to reclaim 19 MB, and would not even reclaim that, since deleting files in an image's lower layers writes whiteouts to the container layer and host usage goes UP. Freeing real host disk from a job means pruning the rootless daemon (`docker image prune -af`, no privileges needed), which `app-e2e`, `dast` and `build-deploy` do; `prod-apk` has no Docker CLI and nothing to prune.

`scripts/__tests__/prod-apk-disk-step.guard.test.mjs` pins the disk-step fix in both directions: it fails any workflow step anywhere in `.forgejo/workflows` that invokes `sudo` in command position, and it fails the `prod-apk` disk step if it deletes `/usr/local/lib/node_modules`, attempts any `rm`, or carries a `|| true` — requiring instead that the step state in its output that no reclamation is attempted and that its name not promise one. It further asserts the commit-status recorder exists, posts under its own context, is `always()` + `continue-on-error`, is off pull requests, reports `<unset>` rather than a wrong value, and matches none of `main`'s required status globs so it cannot gate a merge.

Forgejo runs on the prod daemon (a long-lived service, with Postgres behind it) as the source-of-truth forge, with Actions and the OCI/generic package registry enabled by env; GitHub is a downstream push mirror rather than the source. Every automated consumer authenticates with its own minimally-scoped named personal access token — registry push and pull are split, CD's git write uses a whitelisted-user PAT rather than the runner's auto token (which the pre-receive hook declines on protected `main`), and the debug dispatch token is revoked when idle.

Komodo provides CD to the prod daemon as Core + a Periphery agent + a database, using FerretDB rather than MongoDB (the unpinned Mongo image crash-loops on this new-kernel + rootless combination) and with Periphery repointed at the prod rootless socket. Its webhook is a git-style branch redeploy validated by HMAC with the global webhook secret — it will not consume a posted image digest — so promotion is digest-by-git: CI resolves the immutable digest, commits it to a tracked env file, pushes, then fires the signed webhook, and there is no rollback endpoint (rollback = redeploy the prior digest).

Every literal in the server-setup runbook is a placeholder, and the repository's topology-scrub and secret-scan gates fail the build if a real tailnet host, domain, IP or credential-shaped string lands in git; the runbook also warns that the host-level disaster-recovery snapshot of every stateful service is a different thing from the application's per-user collection backups, with neither replacing the other.

Reboot resilience (Phase 17) is enforced as config-as-code rather than by prose: `scripts/check-prod-restart-policy.mjs` requires `restart: always` on every long-running service in the prod compose files, forbids `restart: unless-stopped` (which does not bring a cleanly stopped container back after a reboot, because the graceful-shutdown drain unit leaves every container at `Exited (0)`), and allows `no`/`on-failure` only for name-matched one-shot containers. The gate runs selftest + scan as the "Prod restart-policy gate" step of the `naming` job in `.forgejo/workflows/guardrails.yml`, so a future prod service added with the obvious `unless-stopped` default cannot silently reintroduce the outage.

Production stack definitions and their deploy order are config-as-code: `infrastructure-as-code/komodo/stacks.toml` holds seven `[[stack]]` blocks that a single Komodo ResourceSync diff-applies, and each block carries `deploy = true` plus an `after` list so applying the sync also *deploys* them in dependency order — `prod-auth` as root, then `prod-mc-service` (waits on Keycloak JWKS), `prod-mcm-bff`, then `prod-movie-assistant` (agents last, since `spreadsheet-mcp` needs the BFF's network and Redis), with `prod-audit` independent, `prod-observability` ordered after the BFF for graph cleanliness only, and `prod-vault` hanging off `prod-auth`.

The Komodo ResourceSync does not create the production stacks from scratch: all four core stacks were created manually during Phase 15 (and the `prod-app → prod-mcm-bff` rename was also done by hand), so the first sync *adopts* the already-live stacks in place as a config diff, which is why the diff is previewed before the first apply.

The Android-emulator job and the Docker-image-building jobs reach `/dev/kvm` by executing directly on the ci host through a host-type Forgejo runner label defined as `kvm:host` (`runs-on: kvm` uses the label *name*), not by passing the device into a job container — that was the setup only until commit `235f2f4c`. What must therefore hold is host state: KVM enabled on the host, the `ci` user in the `kvm` group, and the runner still advertising the label. On this host `/dev/kvm` is mode 666 (`crw-rw-rw- root kvm`, measured 2026-10-12); 660 via a udev rule is the tighter option, and the group membership is what keeps the job working if it is applied. A host job must also provision its own Docker CLI and prove it reaches the `ci` rootless daemon at the job's `DOCKER_HOST` with no fallback socket, and a missing `/dev/kvm` fails the job loudly rather than skipping the mobile suite.

Phase 9 of the server-setup runbook bootstraps `PERIPHERY_ROOT_DIRECTORY` onto persistent disk (a directory under the `prod` user's home) instead of Komodo's stock `/etc/komodo` default, because under rootless Docker `/etc` is copy-up'd to a per-daemon tmpfs: a default Periphery root is wiped on every reboot along with the cloned repo checkout that every stack's relative bind-mounts resolve against, after which Docker auto-creates each missing bind-mount source *file* as a directory and the Mongo and Vault containers fail with `not a directory` (exit 127). Bootstrapping the persistent value at install time is what keeps a rebuild from reintroducing the tmpfs default.

Phase 8's self-hosted Nx remote cache is the open-source Rust `nx-cache-server` binary run as a `prod`-user systemd-user service (like the Actions runner), implementing Nx's built-in custom remote-cache-server API (Nx ≥ 20.8) because the first-party `@nx/s3-cache` / `@nx/shared-fs-cache` packages were deprecated over an unpatchable CVE and must not be used. Its backing S3 object store is RustFS (feature 080), deployed from a host-managed compose under the `prod` user's home on the same pinned image the git-tracked observability stack uses — a pin that must be copied by hand because Renovate never sees the host-managed file — running as the image's own uid, logging to stdout, with the console disabled and only the S3 port published, plus a one-shot init container that PUTs the cache bucket. Client wiring is entirely env-driven (a Forgejo variable for the server URL and a Forgejo secret for the access token, no `nx.json` literal), so local runs without the token fall back to the local cache and no remote-cache config leaks into the repo.

Moving an existing Nx-cache store to RustFS is an in-place, verified copy driven by `scripts/object-store-migration.sh` in ordered stages (`manifest` against the old store's endpoint → `inventory` → `copy --apply` from the old volume to the new → `verify` for parity), with the cache server stopped as the only writer, a one-line rollback (stop the new service, bring the old store up, restore its credentials), and recreating the cache empty accepted as an alternative because the data is rebuildable — a cold cache costs time, not correctness.

The RustFS Nx-cache store is host-managed state, so it has a Renovate blind spot and a host-state trap: its compose lives under the `prod` user's home (like Forgejo, Komodo, cloudflared, beszel, dozzle and uptime-kuma), which Renovate does not see, so its image pin must be copied by hand from the git-tracked RustFS instance in the observability stack whenever that moves; the volume and network names are likewise host state that must be confirmed by ownership *and* contents before the migration copy; and the host backup script captures each store's config directory (never its data volume), so the new store's directory had to be added to that path list too.

The Nx-cache store cutover was performed on prod on 2026-10-21 (spec 080 T044) as a copy rather than a recreate, and the tool's `verify` stage reported 1360 → 1360 objects. The host facts the runbook records alongside it — the previous store's compose project, service, network and volume names, its access key, and the env-file key its secret lived under — are host state that exists nowhere in git.

The host backup script's `restic backup` path list now carries the new Nx-cache store's config directory alongside the previous store's directory, and the previous store's directory stays on that list only until the deferred cleanup (spec 080 T047) removes it — taken off in that same step, because until then it is the rollback. The store's data volume is deliberately never captured: it is rebuildable, and only the config directory is needed to stand the service back up.

The Nx-cache store's access/secret pair lives in two files that must change together: the store's own `.env`, and the cache server's env file, which carries the same pair as its `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`. On this host that env file's endpoint and bucket name were already correct, so the cutover changed only those two credential lines — leaving them behind yields a cache server that starts healthy and cannot read the store.

The Nx-cache store's volume is declared `external: true`, so compose never creates it: only the migration tool's `copy --apply` brings it into existence, with an explicit `docker volume create` on a new host that holds no prior data as the alternative. Referencing the volume before it exists aborts the compose up with an external-volume-not-found error and creates zero containers, so the copy must precede anything that mounts the volume — a deploy fails rather than starting on an empty store.

Two env-file reading traps apply to the store cutover: each store's secret must be extracted from its own env file with a `sed -n` extraction rather than typed into a `read -rs` inside a pasted block, which consumes the next pasted line as its input; and env-file keys must be listed with a pattern that admits digits, because a letters-only pattern silently skips every `S3_…` line.

The `machinectl shell <user>@` requirement is not confined to bring-up: `systemctl --user` and the rootless `docker` CLI both need that user's systemd session (`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, its D-Bus, and the daemon's socket), so every later operation as `prod` — stopping the Nx-cache service, bringing a compose up, enabling a user unit — goes through `sudo machinectl shell prod@` rather than `sudo -iu prod`, which creates none of those and leaves `systemctl --user` failing and `docker` unable to find the daemon.

The host backup script's dump list is the part of Phase 14 that must grow with the host: the original script captured only Forgejo, Komodo and the object-store/cache config directories and no application database at all, so a reboot that corrupted Forgejo's Postgres left Forgejo the only stateful service with a real backup. The standing rule drawn from that incident is that whenever a stateful service is added its dump must be added to `backup.sh` — the same obligation that put the Nx-cache store's config directory on the `restic backup` path list.
